title: Life Insurance Product Types: A Comprehensive Survey

questions.stem: Decreasing term assurance is BEST suited for:

opts.x: Providing income replacement for a family after a breadwinner's death.
Covering a mortgage debt that reduces over time.
Providing a guaranteed maturity benefit at retirement.
Investing in the stock market with life cover as a secondary benefit.

questions.answer: (B) Covering a mortgage debt that reduces over time.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Decreasing term assurance has a sum assured that reduces year by year over the policy term, typically in line with the reducing balance of a capital repayment mortgage. As the outstanding loan decreases — because the borrower is repaying both principal and interest each month — the death benefit reduces correspondingly. This makes decreasing term the most cost-efficient and precisely matched protection product for mortgage borrowers.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Income replacement requires a level death benefit throughout the protection period. If the sum assured is decreasing, surviving dependants receive progressively less cover over time — exactly the wrong profile for income replacement.

(C) Guaranteeing a maturity benefit requires a savings product (endowment or pension) — term assurance of any kind pays only on death within the term; no benefit is payable if the insured survives.

(D) Direct stock market investment is the function of investment-linked life policies, not term assurance. Decreasing term is a pure protection product with no investment or savings element.

questions.stem: Which statement about a whole life assurance policy is CORRECT?

opts.x: The policy expires at the end of a fixed term if no claim has been made.
The policy pays a benefit only if the life assured dies before age 65.
The policy accumulates a cash value and provides lifetime cover.
Premiums decrease as the policyholder gets older.

questions.answer: (C) The policy accumulates a cash value and provides lifetime cover.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

A whole life policy covers the life assured until death — whenever that occurs — unlike term assurance which expires at a fixed date. Because the insured event (death) will certainly occur at some point, the policy must by mathematical necessity accumulate a reserve over time to fund the eventual certain claim. This reserve gives rise to the cash value or surrender value that policyholders can access if they terminate the policy early.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) describes term assurance — a whole life policy has no fixed expiry date; it continues indefinitely until the insured dies.

(B) There is no age 65 cut-off in a whole life policy. The death benefit is payable whenever death occurs — whether at 45 or 95.

(D) Premiums for whole life are typically level (fixed) throughout the premium payment period, not decreasing. In some non-profit designs, premiums may be arranged to cease after a defined period (limited-pay whole life), but they do not reduce as the policyholder ages.

questions.stem: The 'anticipated endowment' or 'money-back policy' is characterised by:

opts.x: Payment of the sum assured only on the life assured's death.
Periodic survival benefit payments during the term, with full death cover maintained throughout.
Investment of premiums directly in stock market funds.
A fixed term of exactly 10 years.

questions.answer: (B) Periodic survival benefit payments during the term, with full death cover maintained throughout.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The money-back policy's defining feature is its dual cash flow structure: it pays defined survival benefits (typically 20% of sum assured) at intervals during the term (years 5, 10, 15) while simultaneously maintaining the full original sum assured as the death benefit throughout the entire policy term. A policyholder who has received two survival payments still receives 100% of the original sum assured if they die before maturity. This combination makes the product uniquely appealing in the Nigerian market.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) describes a pure protection term assurance — the money-back policy's distinguishing commercial feature is precisely that it does pay something during the term to surviving policyholders.

(C) describes an investment-linked life policy. The money-back is a traditional with-profit product; premiums are not directly invested in market funds. Returns come from the insurer's general investment fund, not from specific market-linked units.

(D) Nigerian money-back policies are commonly 15–25 year products. A fixed 10-year term is not definitional and would not accommodate the typical 20%/20%/20%/40% survival benefit structure.

questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025, credit life insurance is MANDATORY for:

opts.x: All employees with a formal employment contract.
All personal loans regardless of amount.
Loans exceeding ₦10 million.
Group life insurance schemes with more than 50 employees.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 Section 91(3) mandates credit life insurance for all qualifying loans exceeding the prescribed threshold of ₦10 million. The credit life policy covers the outstanding loan balance in the event of the borrower's death or total disability, protecting both the lender (who recovers the outstanding debt) and the borrower's estate (which is not burdened with repaying a debt the deceased can no longer service).
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Employment status does not determine the credit life obligation — the size of the loan does. An employee with a ₦5m personal loan has no mandatory credit life obligation under NIIRA 2025; a self-employed borrower with a ₦15m business loan does.

(B) Making all personal loans subject to mandatory credit life regardless of size would impose disproportionate costs on small borrowers. The ₦10m threshold focuses the mandate on material financial exposures.

(D) Group life insurance for employers (PRA 2014 Section 4) is a separate and distinct obligation determined by employee headcount — it has no connection to the credit life insurance mandate.

questions.stem: A waiver of premium rider on an endowment policy:

opts.x: Increases the sum assured if the policyholder reaches age 60.
Waives future premiums if the policyholder becomes totally disabled, keeping the policy in force.
Returns all premiums paid if no claim is made at maturity.
Allows premiums to be paid less frequently without loss of cover.

questions.answer: (B) Waives future premiums if the policyholder becomes totally disabled, keeping the policy in force.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

A waiver of premium (WOP) rider provides that if the policyholder suffers total and permanent disability (as defined in the rider — typically inability to perform own occupation or any occupation, depending on the policy's definition), all future premium obligations are waived. The policy continues in force exactly as if premiums were being paid, but the insurer effectively funds the premium on the disabled policyholder's behalf. On recovery (if the disability is temporary under the policy's terms) or at the end of the waiver period, premiums resume. This is the most economically valuable rider for working-age policyholders who depend on earned income to maintain their policies.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) describes an escalation or guaranteed insurability feature — not a waiver of premium rider.

(C) describes a return-of-premium rider — a separate product feature providing a refund of premiums paid if the insured survives the policy term without making a claim. This is a distinct concept unrelated to disability protection.

(D) describes a premium holiday or flexible payment feature — the ability to pause or reduce premiums. This is not a waiver of premium rider, which is specifically triggered by total disability.

opts.x: By an employee on their own life with a family member as beneficiary.
By a business on the life of a key employee, with the business as beneficiary.
By a government agency to cover civil servants.
By a bank on all mortgage borrowers regardless of loan amount.

questions.answer: (B) By a business on the life of a key employee, with the business as beneficiary.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Keyman insurance (also called key person insurance) is corporate insurance taken out by a business on the life of an individual whose skills, expertise, relationships, or leadership are so central to the business that their death or disability would cause material financial harm. The business is both the policyholder (pays the premium) and the beneficiary (receives the proceeds). The proceeds compensate the business for lost revenue, recruitment and training costs, or loan repayment obligations triggered by the key person's death. NIIRA 2025 recognises keyman insurance as an individual life assurance product.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) describes personal life assurance — the employee owns the policy and nominates a family beneficiary. This is entirely different from keyman insurance, where the insurable interest is the business's financial exposure to the key person's loss.

(C) Government civil servant cover is group life insurance under PRA 2014 or a defined benefit pension scheme — a mandatory employer obligation, not keyman insurance.

(D) describes bank-originated credit life insurance for mortgage borrowers — a separate product category covering loan balance repayment, not business financial loss from losing a key individual.

model.h: Level Term Assurance

(a) Structure: The sum assured is fixed at the level specified at inception and remains constant throughout the policy term. Death benefit is identical in year 1 and year 20.

(b) Nigerian application: Income replacement protection for families with dependants; business partnership protection (covering a fixed liability under a partnership agreement); mortgage protection on interest-only facilities where the outstanding balance remains constant.

(c) Advantage: Simple, transparent, and predictable — the beneficiary knows exactly what will be paid. Limitation: Inflation erodes the real purchasing power of a fixed benefit over long terms. A ₦10m sum assured in 2005 had far greater real value than ₦10m in 2025, given Nigeria's cumulative inflation. No provision for benefit indexation is standard in the Nigerian market.
Decreasing Term Assurance

(a) Structure: The sum assured reduces year by year over the policy term, following a defined schedule (typically mirroring the reducing balance of a repayment loan).

(b) Nigerian application: Repayment mortgage protection (capital-and-interest loan where the outstanding balance reduces each month); credit life insurance mandated by NIIRA 2025 for qualifying loans (covering the reducing outstanding balance); reducing business loan security.

(c) Advantage: Cheaper than level term for the same initial sum assured, because the insurer's exposure reduces over time. Efficiently matched to reducing liabilities — the coverage profile is aligned with the actual financial risk. Limitation: Not suitable for income replacement (where a consistent benefit is needed); the rate of reduction may not perfectly match the actual loan reduction if interest rates change.
Convertible Term Assurance

(a) Structure: A term policy with a contractual option to convert to a permanent policy (whole life or endowment) at the end of the term or at defined intervals, without further medical evidence at conversion.

(b) Nigerian application: Young professionals aged 25–35 who want affordable pure protection now but want to preserve the right to acquire permanent life cover with a savings element when their income grows — regardless of any health deterioration in the interim.

(c) Advantage: Protects future insurability. A policyholder who develops a serious health condition during the term (diabetes, hypertension, cancer) can still convert to a permanent policy because the conversion is on a non-medical basis — the insurer cannot require new medical evidence. This is the product's unique commercial value. Limitation: The conversion premium is based on the insured's attained age at conversion — which may be materially higher than the original term premium, representing a significant additional cost that must be budgeted for.

questions.stem:
Kunle, aged 38, has a ₦5 million 20-year money-back endowment policy that pays 20% of the sum assured at the end of years 5, 10, and 15, with the remaining 40% plus bonuses payable at maturity.
(a) Calculate the survival benefits payable at the end of years 5, 10, and 15.
(b) If Kunle dies in year 12 having already received the year 5 and year 10 survival benefits, what death benefit is payable assuming declared reversionary bonuses of 3.5% per annum simple and no terminal bonus?
(c) Advise Kunle on the advantages and disadvantages of the money-back policy relative to a conventional with-profit endowment with the same premium and term.

model.h: Part (a) — Survival Benefits

The policy pays 20% of the original sum assured at each survival point:

Year 5 survival benefit: 20% × ₦5,000,000 = ₦1,000,000
Year 10 survival benefit: 20% × ₦5,000,000 = ₦1,000,000
Year 15 survival benefit: 20% × ₦5,000,000 = ₦1,000,000

Total survival benefits received during term: ₦3,000,000
Remaining 40% (₦2,000,000) + accrued bonuses: payable at maturity (year 20).
Part (b) — Death Benefit in Year 12

Under a money-back policy, the full original sum assured (100%) is payable on death at any point during the term, regardless of how much has already been paid in survival benefits. The fact that Kunle received ₦1,000,000 at year 5 and ₦1,000,000 at year 10 does NOT reduce the death benefit.

Base sum assured payable on death: ₦5,000,000

Accrued reversionary bonuses (simple, 3.5% pa on original sum assured):
3.5% × ₦5,000,000 × 12 years = ₦175,000 × 12 = ₦2,100,000

Total death benefit payable in year 12: ₦5,000,000 + ₦2,100,000 = ₦7,100,000

Note: No terminal bonus declared (as stated in the question). All outstanding survival benefits that have not yet fallen due are subsumed in the death benefit — Kunle's estate receives the total stated above, not the survival benefits that would have been paid in future years separately.
Part (c) — Money-Back vs Conventional With-Profit Endowment

Money-back advantages for Kunle:
• Liquidity: Three interim cash payments (₦1m each) provide cash at defined intervals — useful for school fees, business investment, or other planned expenses.
• Psychological reassurance: Regular payments provide tangible evidence that 'insurance pays' — addressing the trust deficit.
• Death benefit maintained: Despite interim payouts, full ₦5m death protection is preserved throughout.

Money-back limitations for Kunle:
• Lower maturity value: The conventional endowment accumulates all funds until maturity. The money-back pays out ₦3m during the term, reducing the compounding base. At equivalent premiums, a conventional endowment will typically produce a higher total maturity benefit.
• Return calculation: The internal rate of return on the money-back's survival benefits, when properly discounted, is often lower than it appears because early payments sacrifice compound growth.
• Inflation erosion: Survival benefits are fixed nominal amounts. ₦1,000,000 received in year 5 (when Kunle is 43) has greater purchasing power than ₦1,000,000 received in year 15 (when he is 53).

Advice: If Kunle has near-term liquidity needs (children's education, mortgage payments in years 5–15), the money-back structure is appropriate. If his primary objective is maximising total wealth at age 58 and he does not need interim cash, a conventional endowment with higher bonus accumulation may produce a better total outcome. He should compare actual illustrated values from both products.

questions.stem: Explain the structure and mechanics of an investment-linked life policy (ILP) in Nigeria. Describe the role of the premium allocation rate, the mortality deduction, and the fund management fee. Discuss the circumstances in which an ILP would be more suitable than a conventional endowment policy, and identify the key regulatory disclosure requirements applicable to ILPs under NIIRA 2025.

model.h: ILP Structure and Mechanics

An investment-linked life policy (ILP) is a life assurance product in which a significant proportion of the premium is invested in a defined investment fund — typically a choice of equity, bond, money market, or balanced funds. The policy's value at any time equals the value of the units (shares in the fund) held, rather than a guaranteed sum assured.
The Three Key Charges

1. Premium allocation rate: The proportion of each premium that is actually invested in the fund. Example: an allocation rate of 80% in year 1 means only ₦80,000 of a ₦100,000 premium is invested; the remaining ₦20,000 covers initial expenses and acquisition costs. In later years, the allocation rate typically rises (95–100%), reducing the proportion consumed by charges.

2. Mortality deduction (Cost of Insurance, CoI): Each month, the insurer deducts from the policyholder's fund units the 'cost of insurance' — the pure risk premium for the life cover component. The CoI is calculated as the probability of death in the next month (from the mortality table) multiplied by the net amount at risk (the difference between the sum assured and the current fund value). Critically, the CoI increases with age as mortality risk rises. For older policyholders with small fund values, the escalating CoI can consume the fund rapidly.

3. Fund management fee: An annual charge — typically 1.5–2% of the fund value — deducted in monthly instalments from the policyholder's units. This covers the investment manager's fees and the insurer's ongoing administration costs.
When an ILP is More Suitable Than a Conventional Endowment

An ILP is more suitable when:
• The policyholder has investment sophistication and wants to choose and monitor their fund allocation (equity vs bond vs money market).
• The policyholder values transparency — ILP charges are explicit and itemised; endowment profit margins are embedded in the pricing and less visible.
• The policyholder wants premium flexibility — ILPs can handle irregular premium payments and premium holidays more gracefully than endowments, as long as the fund value is sufficient to sustain the CoI deductions.
• The policyholder has a long time horizon and high risk tolerance — an equity-invested ILP has the potential to outperform a conventional endowment in a sustained bull market.

Conventional endowments are more suitable when the policyholder wants a guaranteed minimum benefit, lower risk, and simpler product terms.
NIIRA 2025 ILP Disclosure Requirements

NIIRA 2025 and the NAICOM product approval guidelines require that ILP proposals are accompanied by:
1. Full explicit disclosure of all charges: premium allocation rate by year, CoI basis, fund management fee, bid-offer spread if applicable.
2. Fund value projections at stated growth rate assumptions AND at a materially lower rate (at least two scenarios).
3. Illustration showing how the CoI increases with age and its potential impact on fund value in later years.
4. Clear statement that the fund value (not the sum assured) determines the maturity benefit, and that poor fund performance could result in the fund being insufficient to sustain the life cover — triggering additional premium demands or cover reduction.

questions.stem: Critically evaluate the anticipated endowment ('money-back policy') as the dominant retail life insurance product in Nigeria. In your answer, analyse the structural, financial, and psychological factors that explain its market dominance, assess its suitability across different consumer segments, and evaluate the extent to which its prevalence serves or undermines the financial inclusion objectives of NIIRA 2025 and NAICOM's microinsurance strategy.

model.h: Thesis

The money-back policy's market dominance reflects a genuine alignment with Nigerian consumer psychology and the realities of an informal economy — but it also reflects the insurance industry's own incentive structures and a distribution model that has historically placed commission revenue above product suitability. The question for a maturing market is whether this dominance advances or impedes financial inclusion.
Structural Factors Explaining Dominance

The money-back's defining structural advantage is its combination of periodic cash returns and maintained death cover. In a market where 'insurance eats money' is a widespread consumer belief, receiving ₦1m back every 5 years is concrete, tangible proof that insurance pays — before the policyholder dies. This trust signal cannot be replicated by any conventional endowment or term product.

The participating bonus structure adds a savings growth narrative that makes the product feel like a dual-purpose financial instrument: protection + savings. This resonates in a market where pure protection products are viewed sceptically and savings-linked products attract higher commitment.
Financial and Psychological Factors

Psychologically, the money-back works because of loss aversion: Nigerian consumers, burned by decades of claims disputes, are far more worried about 'losing' their premiums than they are enthused by the prospect of a long-term benefit. The survival benefit is loss aversion mitigation — you cannot lose all your money because you are getting some back regularly.

Financially, the product's return profile is less attractive than it appears. Survival benefits are fixed nominal amounts that lose real value to Nigeria's chronic inflation. The internal rate of return on money-back policies, when properly calculated, is often below comparable savings instruments. The product's dominance reflects marketing success as much as financial merit.
Suitability Across Consumer Segments

High-income urban professionals: Generally better served by pure term protection (far cheaper for the same cover) plus separate savings or investment products. The money-back is relatively inefficient for this segment — they pay a premium for the periodic payment structure that they could replicate more cheaply and flexibly.

Mid-income formal sector workers: The money-back aligns well — the periodic payments support planned financial commitments (school fees, rent advances), and the discipline of regular premium payment has genuine savings value for this segment.

Low-income informal sector: The premium levels required for meaningful money-back coverage are typically beyond this segment's consistent payment capacity, driving high early lapse rates. This is a mis-suitability risk — the segment that most needs a trust-building product cannot sustain it.
Financial Inclusion Assessment

NIIRA 2025's financial inclusion objectives require extending insurance to the informal sector, rural households, and low-income urban workers — the 170 million uninsured Nigerians. The money-back policy, with its high premium structure, complex benefit architecture, and agent-dependent distribution, is structurally misaligned with these objectives.

NAICOM's microinsurance strategy requires simple, affordable, mobile-distributed products — conceptually the opposite of the money-back. The industry's over-dependence on the money-back is therefore not simply a product design issue; it is a strategic orientation problem. An industry that sells mostly money-back products will reach at best 5–10% of Nigeria's population — precisely the segment that is already partially insured.
Conclusion

NIIRA 2025's TCF framework creates regulatory pressure to sell products that are genuinely suitable for each customer. Applied rigorously, this should reduce money-back sales to lower-income segments where the product's sustained premium demand creates predictable lapse risk. The long-term structural shift required is toward a bifurcated market: money-back and participating endowments for mid-to-high income consumers who can sustain premiums; microinsurance and simple term products for the mass market financial inclusion objective.
Thesis

The mandatory credit life provision in NIIRA 2025 is the most commercially significant single clause in the Act for the life insurance industry's near-term growth. It creates a large, mandatory, and growing pool of insurable exposures at the intersection of Nigeria's most dynamic financial sector (fintech lending) and life insurance's natural market. Its implementation, however, presents product design, regulatory, and operational challenges that will determine whether insurers or fintechs capture the majority of the economic value.
(a) Market Opportunity in Banking and Fintech

Nigeria's total credit stock exceeds ₦30 trillion, with banks and fintechs collectively disbursing hundreds of billions of naira annually in loans qualifying above the ₦10m threshold (SME loans, mortgage facilities, corporate facilities). Every qualifying loan originated after NIIRA 2025's commencement date requires a credit life policy — creating a mandatory premium flow.

The fintech dimension is particularly significant: Nigerian digital lenders (Carbon, FairMoney, Branch, Kuda) are originating rapidly growing loan volumes to segments that conventional insurance has never reached. Embedding credit life at loan origination — automatically priced into the loan and bundled with disbursement — is the most frictionless distribution mechanism the industry has ever had access to.

Estimated market size: If the qualifying loan book subject to NIIRA 2025 credit life is ₦10 trillion, and credit life premium rates average 0.3–0.5% pa of outstanding balance, the addressable annual premium pool is ₦30–50 billion — a material increment to the Nigerian life insurance market.
(b) Protection of Borrowers' Families

The credit life mandate addresses a significant and previously unaddressed protection gap: the death of a loan borrower frequently results in the outstanding debt burden being inherited by the family — often precipitating loss of family home (mortgage), loss of business assets (SME loan), or harassment by debt collectors.

With mandatory credit life in force, the insurer settles the outstanding loan balance on death, freeing the borrower's estate and family from the debt. This is particularly valuable for SME borrowers whose entire family business may be secured against a single qualifying loan.

Limitation: Coverage is limited to the outstanding loan balance — it does not replace the borrower's income or provide any additional protection for dependants. Credit life is not a substitute for personal life insurance.
(c) Implementation Challenges

1. Product design: Credit life must have a reducing sum assured that mirrors the actual loan balance at each point. For revolving credit facilities, this requires real-time or regular reporting of the outstanding balance — a significant data integration challenge.

2. Pricing: Credit life for fintech lending populations — often the 'thin file' segment without formal credit history — requires actuarial data that Nigerian life insurers do not currently possess. Adverse selection and moral hazard are genuine pricing risks.

3. Lender-insurer regulatory split: The lender is not a licensed insurer; the insurer is not a licensed lender. The embedded credit life arrangement requires a clearly documented agency or partnership agreement compliant with both NIIRA 2025 and CBN regulations. The boundary between insurance premium collection and loan interest cannot be blurred.

4. Disclosure to borrowers: NIIRA 2025 requires that borrowers are clearly informed they are purchasing insurance (including the name of the insurer, the premium, and the coverage terms) and must not simply find the credit life premium embedded in the loan repayment without explanation.
Opportunities and Risks for Embedded Insurance

Opportunities: Credit life establishes the embedded insurance relationship. Once an insurer is integrated into a lender's origination platform and has demonstrated reliable claims payment, cross-selling additional products (personal life, health) to the borrower base becomes operationally feasible.

Risks: The insurer who wins the credit life mandate by offering the lowest price — a common Nigerian insurance market dynamic — may be pricing unsustainably. If claims experience on a fintech borrower portfolio is worse than assumed (as it may well be for thin-file borrowers), losses on the credit life book could damage the insurer's solvency.
